content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

I'm the facilitator for this project, and we're at the very start — understanding what you really want before anything gets built. Let me begin by understanding the goal itself, not the technical side.

You said you want to save and manage bookmarks. Before we talk about *how*, I'd like to understand *why*:

**When this app is finished and working well, what would be different about your day compared to now?** For example — is the pain that your bookmarks are scattered across different browsers and you can never find them again? That you save things and forget they exist? That you want to organize links for a specific purpose (research, work projects, sharing with others)?

What's the situation today that makes you want this?

Right now I save links in different browser folders, then struggle to find them later or forget why I saved them. I want one personal place where I can quickly save a link, have its basic details filled in automatically, add tags or a note, and later find it through search or filters. I’d also like to mark things to read later and archive links I want to keep without cluttering the main list.

content:
That's really clear, thank you. Let me play back what I understood to make sure I've got the direction right:

Today your links are spread across browser folders, and the real pain is two-sided: **you can't find things again**, and even when you do, **you've forgotten why you saved them**. So what you actually want isn't just "a place to store links" — it's **one personal place where saving is quick and finding-again is reliable**, so links stop getting lost.

Around that core, you described these needs:
- **Save fast** — drop in a link with minimal effort
- **Details filled in automatically** — so you don't have to type out what the link is
- **Add your own tags or a note** — capture *why* it mattered
- **Find it later** — through search or filters
- **Read-later marking** — flag things you intend to get to
- **Archive** — keep links long-term without cluttering your main list

One thing I want to check on the goal level: is the heart of this **"never lose a saved link again"** (reliable capture + retrieval), and everything else — tags, read-later, archive — is in service of that? Or is one of those, say read-later, actually its own main purpose for you?

And a second question: this is **just for you personally**, not something you'll share with a team or others — did I read that right?

Yes, the main goal is reliable capture and retrieval—being able to save something quickly and actually find and understand it later. Read-later and archiving support that rather than being separate purposes.

And yes, this is a personal app just for me; I don’t need team sharing.

Is a gentle fallback like that what you'd want, or would you rather it show nothing until the query is valid?
- A bare word like `dev` (no `#`) matches it **anywhere** — including as a tag — while `#dev` restricts to the tag specifically. Does that distinction match your mental model?

How does searching feel now — does it cover the precision you were after?

Yes, this covers the search precision I wanted. The gentle fallback is preferable to an empty result or error wall while I’m still typing, especially with live search. The distinction between a broad bare-word search and `#dev` meaning that specific tag also feels clear and useful.

That's the last piece. Here's everything we've settled together, in plain terms — this is the scope I'd build.

**Saving & automatic details**
- Paste a link and save it in one step; it appears at the top of your list.
- The title, description, site icon, and a preview image (when the page has one) are filled in automatically. If a page's details can't be read, the link is still saved and you can type them in yourself.

**Organizing**
- Add tags and a note while saving (both optional), with suggestions from tags you already use and an easy way to create new ones.
- Edit a bookmark's title, description, tags, note, or even its link later — changing the link can optionally refresh the details.
- Notes are written in Markdown and shown nicely formatted.

**Keeping the list useful**
- Mark things "Read later" and see just those; archive links to keep them without cluttering the main list; restore or delete (with a brief undo) as needed.
- Three views — All, To read, Archived — each with a count.
- Sort by newest, oldest, title, or recently updated.

**Finding again**
- A powerful search across title, description, note, tags, and link — with exact phrases, tag-specific searches, and AND/OR/NOT with grouping — plus a tag filter bar. Save any search (query + filter + view) to reuse with one click.

**Working in bulk**
- Select several bookmarks, or everything in the current view, to tag, untag, mark read/unread, archive, or delete together.

**Keeping copies safe**
- Preserve a full-page copy of a bookmark (kept as a self-contained file; PDFs kept as PDFs), automatically or on demand, and optionally also save it to the Internet Archive.

**Moving in and out**
- Import your browser's bookmarks (folders become tags, duplicates skipped, original titles/dates/tags preserved) and export as a browser file or a full backup.

**Comfort**
- Display preferences: light/dark/match-system, density, text size, show/hide previews, how many per page (with paging), which view to open on, and default sort.

It's a personal, single-user web app, and we've walked through the empty, error, overflow, and duplicate situations for these along the way.

**May I start building this scope now?** Once you approve, I'll switch into development and implement exactly what we've confirmed here.

## Your bookmark manager is built and ready to review

**Open it at:** http://maker:4000 — it starts on a clean, empty library (your real first-run), and since it's a live app you can paste in real links and watch the details fill in automatically.

### What was built
Everything we agreed, implemented fresh from the behaviours you approved (25 scenarios) — saving with automatic details, tags & Markdown notes, editing everything later, read-later/archive, powerful search + tag filter + saved searches, sorting, bulk actions, full-page & PDF copies plus Internet Archive, browser import/export, display preferences with paging, and all the empty/error/duplicate/overflow cases.

### Verification — passed
- **Behaviour (acceptance) tests: 35/35 passed.** An automated browser drives the real app through every approved scenario — saving, the duplicate-and-edit flow, the unreadable-page fallback, the full search grammar (phrases, `#tag`, AND/OR/NOT, graceful fallback), read-later/archive, delete-with-undo, bulk actions, snapshots, Internet Archive, import (preserving titles/dates/tags), export, preferences and paging.
- **Internal tests: 34/34 passed.** Covering the search engine, Markdown renderer, import/export, and all the data operations against a controlled test site.
- **Live check:** a real save of a public page fetched its title correctly, with no errors.
- During testing I found and fixed two genuine defects: duplicate-detection was ignoring query strings, and the search highlighter mis-handled single-letter terms — both corrected and re-verified.

A couple of honesty notes: the automatic details, page snapshots, and Internet Archive step reach out to the live internet, so their results depend on the target site and that service being reachable; when something can't be fetched, the app saves the link anyway and lets you retry, exactly as we agreed.
